## D.4 New Experiments on Gemma

We further validate SpecDec++ by repeating all the experiments on a new pair of models: Gemma-1.1-2B-it (Team et al., 2024a) and Gemma-2-27B-it (Team et al., 2024b). The Pareto frontiers of verification rates versus discard rates are plotted in Figure 5, and the empirical speedup is reported in Table 4. Specifically, we see that

- SpecDec++ has better Pareto frontiers in terms of discard rates v.s. verification rates tradeoff than the baseline SpecDec algorithm on the Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval datasets. The Pareto improvement indicates that SpecDec++ will have better speedups than SpecDec under arbitrary hardware configurations.

- When deployed on 1 Nvidia A100-80G GPU, SpecDec++ achieves a relative 1.4%, 12.4% and 7.7% improvement over the baseline methods on the Alpaca, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, respectively. Figure 5: The average verification rates $N_{\mathrm{target}}/N$ and the average discard rates $N_{\mathrm{discarded}}/N$ for SpecDec with different candidate lengths and SpecDec++ with different acceptance prediction heads and stopping thresholds. SpecDec++ has better Pareto frontiers than SpecDec on both the in-distribution dataset Alpaca and the two out-of-distribution datasets HumanEval and GSM8K. The model pair is Gemma-1.1-2B-it/Gemma-2-27B-it. We observe fewer improvements on the Alpaca dataset and the GSM8K dataset compared to the llama-2-7b-chat/llama-2-70b-chat model pair. This phenomenon may be caused by weaker alignment between the draft Gemma model and the target Gemma model. On Alpaca, the baseline SpecDec achieves 1.33x speedup for the Gemma model pair but it achieves 1.90x speedup for the Llama model pair; on GSM8K, the baseline SpecDec achieves 1.47x speedup for the Gemma model pair but it achieves 2.07x speedup for the Llama model pair. We see our chosen Gemma model pair performs worse than the Llama model pair, although the model size ratios are roughly the same for the two model families (27B/2B v.s. 70B/7B).

We suspect that for the Gemma-1.1-2B-it and Gemma-2-27B-it model pair on the Alpaca dataset, our acceptance prediction head ends up suggesting an approximately fixed draft length, therefore only achieving a small improvement over the baseline. For settings like math (GSM8K) and coding (HumanEval), the generation involves a mixture of tokens of verbal reasoning and tokens of math calculation/code writing, which naturally require an adaptive draft length.

In summary, although the specific numbers of the improvement vary across different model pairs and different prompt settings, the proposed SpecDec++ indeed achieves an adequate amount of improvements over the baseline. Backed by the theoretical results, our proposed method is a principled extension of the SpecDec method, and adaptively determining the draft length naturally includes the baseline (a fixed draft length) as a special case.

In the section, we present the proof of Theorem 4.3.

For any time-homogeneous policy $\pi$ , we define a random variable $C^{\pi}(s,a)$ as the total cost-to-go from the current state $s=\left(x_{\mathrm{prefix}},\left(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k}\right)\right)$ when taking action a.

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, a) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} c \left(s _ {i}, a _ {i}, s _ {i + 1}\right), \mathrm {w i t h} s _ {1} = s, a _ {1} = a,
$$

where the next state $s_{i+1}$ given $(s_{i}, a_{i})$ follows the stochastic transition of the MDP, $a_{i}=\pi(s_{i})$ for $i \geq 2$ , and M is a random variable of the number of total steps. We make the assumption that $\pi$ has an upper bound for the number of candidate tokens, so we exclude the cases where the policy $\pi$ potentially leads to an infinite loop and hence $M<\infty$ . Let $C^{\pi}(s)=C^{\pi}(s,\pi(s))$

proof of Theorem 4.3. We analyze the difference $C^{\pi}(s,\mathrm{continue})-C^{\pi}(s,\mathrm{stop})$ for three cases. Case 1. $\mathcal{E}_{1}=\{\exists 1\leq i\leq k+1$ , such that $Y_{i}$ is rejected}.

Let $x_{\mathrm{prefix}}^{\prime}$ be the next prefix given by the speculative decoding algorithm, where the first rejected token among $( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1})$ is replaced by the token from the modified distribution. We know that

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) = c _ {1} + c _ {2} + C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(x _ {\mathrm {p r e f i x}} ^ {\prime}, \varnothing\right)\right).
$$

If we choose to continue at the current step, we know that no matter how many additional steps we continue to generate draft tokens, we will eventually discard them and get the same new prefix $x_{\mathrm{prefix}}^{\prime}$ . Let $N_{\mathrm{continue}}^{\pi}(s)$ be the total number of extra continue's induced by the policy $\pi$ given the current state s and action continue. We have

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {c o n t i n u e}) = c _ {1} + c _ {1} \cdot \left(1 + N _ {\mathrm {c o n t i n u e}} ^ {\pi} (s)\right) + c _ {2} + C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(x _ {\mathrm {p r e f i x}} ^ {\prime}, \varnothing\right)\right).
$$

In summary, we have

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {c o n t i n u e}) - C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) \geq c _ {1}, \mathrm {c o n d i t i o n e d} \mathrm {o n} \mathcal {E} _ {1}
$$

Case 2. $\mathcal{E}_{2}=\{\forall1\leq i\leq k+1, Y_{i}$ is accepted, $Y_{k+2}$ is rejected}.

If we stop the current round of speculation, then all the candidate tokens $( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1} )$ will be accepted and an additional $X_{k+2}$ is sampled from $p ( \cdot\mid x_{\mathrm{prefix}},Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1})$

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) = c _ {2} + C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(\left(x _ {\mathrm {p r e f i x}}, Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k + 1}, X _ {k + 2}\right), \varnothing\right)\right).
$$

Again, if we choose to continue at the current step, as $Y_{k+2}$ is rejected, future generated tokens beyond $Y_{k+2}$ will also be discarded. After the verification, $Y_{k+2}$ will be replaced by $W_{k+2}\sim \mathrm{Norm}[(p(\cdot|x_{\mathrm{prefix}},Y_{1}\dots,Y_{k+1})-q(\cdot|x_{\mathrm{prefix}},Y_{1}\dots,Y_{k+1}))_{+}]$ . Let $N_{\mathrm{continue}}^{\pi}(s)$ be the total number of extra continue's induced by the policy $\pi$ given the current state s and action continue. We have

$$
C ^ {\pi} \left(s, \text {c o n t i n u e}\right) = c _ {1} \cdot \left(1 + N _ {\text {c o n t i n u e}} ^ {\pi} (s)\right) + c _ {2} + C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(\left(x _ {\text {p r e f i x}}, Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k + 1}, W _ {k + 2}\right), \varnothing\right)\right).
$$

Denote $\Delta_{1}=C^{\pi}(( ( x_{\mathrm{prefix}}, Y_{1}, \dots, Y_{k+1}, X_{k+2}),\varnothing))-C^{\pi}(( ( x_{\mathrm{prefix}}, Y_{1}, \dots, Y_{k+1}, W_{k+2}),\varnothing))$ In summary, we have

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {c o n t i u e}) - C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) \geq c _ {1} - \Delta_ {1}, \mathrm {c o n d i t i o n e d} \mathrm {o n} \mathcal {E} _ {2}
$$

Case 3. $\mathcal{E}_{3}=\{\forall1\leq i\leq k+2, Y_{i}$ is accepted}.

Case 3. $\mathcal{E}_{3}=\{\forall1\leq i\leq k+2, Y_{i}$ is accepted}.

Similar to Case 2, if we stop the current round of speculation, then all the candidate tokens $( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1} )$ will be accepted, and an additional $X_{k+2}$ is sampled from $p(\cdot | x_{\mathrm{prefix}},Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1})$

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) = c _ {2} + C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(\left(x _ {\mathrm {p r e f i x}}, Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k + 1}, X _ {k + 2}\right), \varnothing\right)\right).
$$

If we choose to continue at the current step, there is no immediate cost at the current step and we transit to $( x_{\mathrm{prefix}},( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k+1}) )$

$$
C ^ {\pi} (s, \text {c o n t i n u e}) = C ^ {\pi} \left(\left(x _ {\text {p r e f i x}} , \left(Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k + 1}\right)\right)\right).
$$

$\Delta_{2}=C^{\pi}(( ( x_{\mathrm{prefix}}, Y_{1}, \dots, Y_{k+1}, X_{k+2}), \varnothing))-C^{\pi}(( ( x_{\mathrm{prefix}}, ( Y_{1}, \dots, Y_{k+1}) )))$ We have

$C^{\pi}(s,\mathrm{continue})-C^{\pi}(s,\mathrm{stop})\geq -c_{2}-\Delta_{2},$ conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{3}.$

Summary. At the current state, the values of $( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k} )$ are known. We calculate the conditional expectation of $C^{\pi}(s, \mathrm{continue})-C^{\pi}(s,\mathrm{stop})$ given the current observation. For simplicity of notation, we do not explicitly write out the condition on $( Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k} )$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {E} \left[ C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {c o n t i n u e}) - C ^ {\pi} (s, \mathrm {s t o p}) \right] \\ \geq \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) c _ {1} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) \left(c _ {1} - \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {1} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {2} \right]\right) + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) \left(- c _ {2} - \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {2} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {3} \right]\right). \\ \end{array}
$$

When the right-hand side of the above inequality is larger than zero, the expected total cost of continue is larger than the expected cost of stop. Therefore, we obtain a sufficient condition to stop at the current step.

To continue the analysis, we assume that we have an almost-sure upper bound $\Delta$ on $\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}_{2}]$ and $\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{2}\mid\mathcal{E}_{3}]$:

$$
\mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {1} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {2} \right] \leq \Delta a. s. \text {a n d} \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {2} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {3} \right] \leq \Delta a. s..
$$

A naive bound for $\Delta$ is the upper bound of C, e.g., $\max N_{\mathrm{target}}\cdot t_{\mathrm{target}}+\max N_{\mathrm{draft}}\cdot t_{\mathrm{draft}}.$ We assume that both the maximum generated tokens and the numbers of candidate tokens per round have an upper limit, so the upper bound is finite.

Then

\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) c _ {1} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) \left(c _ {1} - \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {1} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {2} \right]\right) + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) \left(- c _ {2} - \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {2} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {3} \right]\right) \geq 0 \\ \Leftrightarrow \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) c _ {1} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) c _ {1} \geq \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) c _ {2} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {2} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {3} \right] + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) \mathbb {E} \left[ \Delta_ {1} \mid \mathcal {E} _ {2} \right] \\ \Leftrightarrow \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) c _ {1} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) c _ {1} \geq \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) c _ {2} + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {3}\right) \Delta + \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {2}\right) \Delta \\ \Leftrightarrow \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) c _

. \\ \end{array}

Finally, we note that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbb {P} \left(\mathcal {E} _ {1}\right) = \mathbb {P} [ \exists 1 \leq i \leq k + 1, \text {s u c h t h a t} Y _ {i} \text {i s r e j e c t e d} \mid Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k} ] \\ \geq \mathbb {P} [ \exists 1 \leq i \leq k, \text {s u c h t h a t} Y _ {i} \text {i s r e j e c t e d} \mid Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {k} ], \\ \end{array}
$$

which concludes the proof.
